ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Interestingly, previous studies point to source trustworthiness as one such condition. Priester and Petty (1995; 2003) found that participants were less likely to distinguish between strong and weak arguments when these arguments were advanced by trustworthy sources.

> By contrast, argument quality was more readily perceived when subjects were exposed to arguments from untrustworthy sources.

> Participants were asked to evaluate a series of political arguments which appealed to various authoritative sources in politics as a means to support the advanced standpoints.

> Participants were presented with only one version of each argument.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Trusting More, Questioning Less? Political trust and receptivity to arguments from authority in political communication

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

text.text: Political trust sustains democratic cooperation, but it may also reflect a broader tendency to align with those in power.
If politically trusting individuals are more inclined to defer to political authority, can they remain critical of the information authorities provide?
In this pre-registered survey experiment, participants (N= 1010) evaluated a series of political arguments from authority, classified as either normatively sound or fallacious.
Political trust consistently predicted argument acceptability, without compromising evaluative accuracy.
However, we found that trust was negatively correlated with soundness discrimination among participants who reported a stronger interest in politics.
Exploratory analyses further showed that trust had a similar negative effect when participants registered identical ratings of trustworthiness for different political institutions.

Together, these findings suggest that political trust may increase the persuasiveness of arguments from political authorities and that, under certain conditions, this effect may come at a cost of critical evaluation.

Political trust, generally defined as the public's confidence in political institutions (Bobzien, 2023), is often framed as an essential condition for democracy (Easton, 1975; Mishler & Rose, 2001; Turper & Aarts, 2015).
text.formatted: Political trust, generally defined as the public's confidence in political institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bobzien, 2023)</ref>, is often framed as an essential condition for democracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Easton, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Mishler & Rose, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Turper & Aarts, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Several behavioral outcomes associated with political trust are conducive to democratic governance, such as greater voter turnout and stronger support for government policies (Devine, 2024; Levi & Stoker, 2000; Li et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Several behavioral outcomes associated with political trust are conducive to democratic governance, such as greater voter turnout and stronger support for government policies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Devine, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Levi & Stoker, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Li et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A broader pattern that emerges from the literature is that politically trusting individuals appear more willing to defer to political authority and comply with institutional directives.
This pattern is also expressed attitudinally.

Studies on authoritarianism and system justification find a positive association with political trust, such that politically trusting individuals are more likely to hold authoritarian attitudes (Dunn, 2020; Jamil & Baniamin, 2020; Miranda et al., 2022; Pernia, 2021; Pernia & Rye, 2025) and more likely to legitimize authority, hierarchy and systemic power (Friesen et al., 2018; Kelemen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Studies on authoritarianism and system justification find a positive association with political trust, such that politically trusting individuals are more likely to hold authoritarian attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dunn, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Jamil & Baniamin, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Miranda et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Pernia, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pernia & Rye, 2025)</ref> and more likely to legitimize authority, hierarchy and systemic power <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Friesen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kelemen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these behavioral and attitudinal correlates suggest that political trust is associated with a broader tendency to support social and political authority.
This association has the potential to undermine the democratic function of political trust.

While collective confidence in governance can enhance societal cohesion and facilitate effective policymaking, democracy also depends on a vigilant citizenry whose skepticism acts as a safeguard against the erosion of accountability and protects against undesirable state activities (Norris, 2022).
text.formatted: While collective confidence in governance can enhance societal cohesion and facilitate effective policymaking, democracy also depends on a vigilant citizenry whose skepticism acts as a safeguard against the erosion of accountability and protects against undesirable state activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Norris, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: If political trust implies a systematically positive attitude toward political authorities (Hadarics, 2025), it may also affect how individuals engage with these authorities in the information environment.
text.formatted: If political trust implies a systematically positive attitude toward political authorities <ref type="bibr">(Hadarics, 2025)</ref>, it may also affect how individuals engage with these authorities in the information environment.

text.text: When citizens are inclined to align with those in power they could be proportionally less inclined to question the claims, decisions and information communicated by the political status quo.

To explore whether political trust can have such negative implications, we need to move beyond behavioral and attitudinal accounts and towards the domain of information processing and informal reasoning.

Certain studies suggest that political trust often predicts reduced evaluative scrutiny across various contexts (Hadarics, 2025; Rossini et al., 2023; Trumbo & McComas, 2008; van Zoonen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Certain studies suggest that political trust often predicts reduced evaluative scrutiny across various contexts <ref type="bibr">(Hadarics, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rossini et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Trumbo & McComas, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">van Zoonen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This line of research frames political trust as an epistemic cue with negative implications for the critical evaluation of political authorities and of communicated information.

At the same time, research on misinformation and conspiracy theories indicates that trust reduces susceptibility to low-quality information (Giancola et al., 2025; Jedinger & Masch, 2025; Zimmermann & Kohring, 2020), such that politically trusting individuals are less likely to endorse false news and conspiratorial beliefs.
text.formatted: At the same time, research on misinformation and conspiracy theories indicates that trust reduces susceptibility to low-quality information <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Giancola et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Jedinger & Masch, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Zimmermann & Kohring, 2020)</ref>, such that politically trusting individuals are less likely to endorse false news and conspiratorial beliefs.

text.text: These findings need not be empirically contradictory.
Existing studies differ substantially in how they operationalize low-quality information and, consequently, in the normative expectations against which critical thinking is assessed.

While in some studies, low-quality information consists of anti-establishment narratives and misinformation originating from non-authoritative sources (Jedinger & Masch, 2025; Zimmermann & Kohring, 2020), other studies consider political authorities as sources of misinformation (Rossini et al., 2023; Trumbo & McComas, 2008).
text.formatted: While in some studies, low-quality information consists of anti-establishment narratives and misinformation originating from non-authoritative sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Jedinger & Masch, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Zimmermann & Kohring, 2020)</ref>, other studies consider political authorities as sources of misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Rossini et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Trumbo & McComas, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Given the connection between political trust and support for authority, the same evaluative strategy -endorsement of authoritative sources in politics -could be interpreted as increased epistemic vigilance in some paradigms but as decreased epistemic vigilance in others.
This makes it difficult to establish whether political trust is associated with sensitivity to information quality or simply determines receptivity to political authority.
In the present study, we address this gap in prior literature by exploring the trust-authority relationship in political communication.
To that end, we focus on a particularly relevant communicative scenario, namely argumentation from authority.

If political trust captures evaluative processes that place greater importance on the claims and opinions of authoritative sources in politics, then we can expect that arguments from authority, and in particular arguments from political authority, will reflect this trend.

More importantly, the normative distinction between sound and fallacious appeals to authority allows us to explore whether political trust predicts the quality of reasoning in political communication.

While previous paradigms obscure the distinction between receptivity to authority and sensitivity to information quality, the argumentation framework allows those dimensions to be isolated because authoritative standing can be preserved within an argument while the soundness of reliance on that particular authority varies.

This approach provides a more direct test of the association between political trust and endorsement of authority, thereby clarifying its broader implications for critical reasoning in political communication.
Arguments from authority are defined as claims supported primarily by the status of the argument's source (Andone & Hernández, 2019).
text.formatted: Arguments from authority are defined as claims supported primarily by the status of the argument's source <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andone & Hernández, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: From a pragma-dialectical perspective, such arguments rest on a symptomatic scheme in which the acceptability of a standpoint is supported by presenting its endorsement by an authoritative source as a sign of its acceptability.

In its basic structure, this scheme includes a premise stating that an authoritative source asserts or endorses a proposition and a conclusion stating that the proposition should therefore be accepted (van Eemeren & Grootendorst, 1992; van Eemeren et al., 2007).
text.formatted: In its basic structure, this scheme includes a premise stating that an authoritative source asserts or endorses a proposition and a conclusion stating that the proposition should therefore be accepted <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(van Eemeren & Grootendorst, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">van Eemeren et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: By consequence, the persuasive force of arguments from authority depends, at least in part, on the recipient's willingness to acknowledge the cited authority as reliable.

When people decide whether to accept a message as true or reject it as false, they often do so based on the characteristics of the message's source (Booth-Butterfield & Gutowski, 1993; Guillory & Geraci, 2013; Henkel & Mattson, 2011; Koh & Sundar, 2010; Priester & Petty, 2003).
text.formatted: When people decide whether to accept a message as true or reject it as false, they often do so based on the characteristics of the message's source <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Booth-Butterfield & Gutowski, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Guillory & Geraci, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Henkel & Mattson, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Koh & Sundar, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Priester & Petty, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Generally, perceiving a source as trustworthy makes people more likely to perceive the information communicated by that source as reliable (Meinert & Kramer, 2022; Koh & Sundar, 2010).
text.formatted: Generally, perceiving a source as trustworthy makes people more likely to perceive the information communicated by that source as reliable <ref type="bibr">(Meinert & Kramer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Koh & Sundar, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the concept of trust is particularly relevant in the context of argumentation from authority.
Because audiences ascribe greater epistemic weight to information communicated by trusted sources, they are more likely to accept argumentative premises endorsed by authorities they trust.
Greater acceptance of an argumentative premise, in turn, provides stronger grounds for accepting the conclusion that follows from it.
Hence, the acceptability of arguments from authority increases when an argument appeals to an authoritative source that is perceived as trustworthy.

Traditional measures of political trust are based on self-reported trust in political authorities such as the government, political parties and courts of justice, typically using Likerttype scales and combining several items into an aggregated trust score (Eurobarometer, 2023; European Social Survey, 2018; 2020; Smets et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Traditional measures of political trust are based on self-reported trust in political authorities such as the government, political parties and courts of justice, typically using Likerttype scales and combining several items into an aggregated trust score <ref type="bibr">(Eurobarometer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">European Social Survey, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Smets et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In political science and social psychology these measures reflect an evaluative attitude toward the political system and its various institutions (Levi & Stoker, 2000).
text.formatted: In political science and social psychology these measures reflect an evaluative attitude toward the political system and its various institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Levi & Stoker, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Within the context of political communication however, the same measures could also capture an epistemic orientation.
Given that source trustworthiness serves as an epistemic cue, measures of political trust should predict the perceived credibility of statements made or endorsed by political authorities.
When these authorities appear as argument sources, political trust is expected to function as a source cue.
We thus hypothesize that political trust will positively predict the acceptability of arguments from authority which appeal to a political entity as an authoritative source.
H1: As political trust increases, arguments from political authority become more acceptable.
Reliance on source cues is often an efficient and rational evaluative strategy.
Sometimes there is little choice but to accept information on the basis of someone else's claims.
For instance, there are topics which require so much specialized knowledge that laypeople cannot independently verify them (van Eemeren & Snoeck Henkemans, 2017).
text.formatted: For instance, there are topics which require so much specialized knowledge that laypeople cannot independently verify them <ref type="bibr">(van Eemeren & Snoeck Henkemans, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, this strategy can become problematic if used as a default response.
That is, if reasoners outsource evaluative judgments to authority without considering the substance of the advanced claim (Meinert & Krammer, 2022).
text.formatted: That is, if reasoners outsource evaluative judgments to authority without considering the substance of the advanced claim <ref type="bibr">(Meinert & Krammer, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To derive accurate conclusions from authority arguments, an audience must sufficiently engage with their content to determine whether reliance on authoritative sources is warranted in the first place.
This is especially important when arguments appeal to political authorities.
By default, political actors possess authoritative standing in view of their recognized role in public decision-making.
This form of authority is defined as 'deontic authority' and it describes individuals or institutions authorized to formulate directives (Brozek, 2013; Koszowy & Walton, 2019).
text.formatted: This form of authority is defined as 'deontic authority' and it describes individuals or institutions authorized to formulate directives <ref type="bibr">(Brozek, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Koszowy & Walton, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Deontic authority is conceptually distinct from epistemic authority, which is grounded in a source's knowledge or expertise (ibid.).
While the two types of authority may happen to overlap in some cases, epistemic authority cannot be automatically inferred from deontic authority.
However, this inference could occur in the context of political argumentation if audiences perceive political actors as authoritative by default.
It follows that reasoners should distinguish between deontic and epistemic aspects of authority when assessing argument acceptability.
Dialectical approaches to argumentation provide a framework for this exact task.

The soundness of arguments from authority is determined through a series of critical questions aimed at identifying whether the cited source possesses genuine authority, whether their expertise is relevant to the topic under discussion and whether their claim has evidentiary support (Wagemans, 2011; Walton, 2014).
text.formatted: The soundness of arguments from authority is determined through a series of critical questions aimed at identifying whether the cited source possesses genuine authority, whether their expertise is relevant to the topic under discussion and whether their claim has evidentiary support <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Wagemans, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walton, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: If one or several of these criteria are not met, then the argument constitutes a fallacy.

One such fallacy is 'abuse of authority' (argumentum ad verecundiam), where the cited source is credited with an authority they do not actually possess, or the authority's domain is not relevant in the particular context in which it is invoked (van Eemeren & Garssen, 2023; Wagemans, 2011).
text.formatted: One such fallacy is 'abuse of authority' (argumentum ad verecundiam), where the cited source is credited with an authority they do not actually possess, or the authority's domain is not relevant in the particular context in which it is invoked <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(van Eemeren & Garssen, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Wagemans, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Another possible fallacy in authority argumentation relates to 'populist argumentation' (argumentum ad populum), upon which the view of the majority is presented as sufficient proof for a claim's acceptability (e.g.
"If many people believe X, then X must be correct") while failing to demonstrate the relevance of the majority appeal (Andone, 2016; Godden, 2008).
text.formatted: "If many people believe X, then X must be correct") while failing to demonstrate the relevance of the majority appeal <ref type="bibr">(Andone, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Godden, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction between sound arguments and fallacies offers a normative benchmark for measuring sensitivity to variations in argument quality.
When people evaluate arguments based on their merits, sound arguments should elicit more favorable evaluations than fallacies.
Understanding when and why individuals fail to make that distinction therefore allows us to determine the conditions that reduce argument scrutiny.

Interestingly, previous studies point to source trustworthiness as one such condition. Priester and Petty (1995; 2003) found that participants were less likely to distinguish between strong and weak arguments when these arguments were advanced by trustworthy sources.
text.formatted: Interestingly, previous studies point to source trustworthiness as one such condition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Priester and Petty (1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">2003)</ref> found that participants were less likely to distinguish between strong and weak arguments when these arguments were advanced by trustworthy sources.

text.text: By contrast, argument quality was more readily perceived when subjects were exposed to arguments from untrustworthy sources.

Research on epistemic vigilance explains this pattern by proposing that humans tend to avoid the cognitive cost of effortful processing unless they are motivated by situational factors to do otherwise (Sperber et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Research on epistemic vigilance explains this pattern by proposing that humans tend to avoid the cognitive cost of effortful processing unless they are motivated by situational factors to do otherwise <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Sperber et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, trust in a source can reduce the perceived need to critically examine communicated information (Levy, 2022; Mayo, 2015).
text.formatted: In this context, trust in a source can reduce the perceived need to critically examine communicated information <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Levy, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mayo, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Given that source trustworthiness is generally translated as informational credibility, individuals presented with claims from trusted sources are not situationally motivated to scrutinize the substance of these claims and, instead, tend to accept information at face value (Mayo, 2015).
text.formatted: Given that source trustworthiness is generally translated as informational credibility, individuals presented with claims from trusted sources are not situationally motivated to scrutinize the substance of these claims and, instead, tend to accept information at face value <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mayo, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: An unreliable source on the other hand, invites more cognitive deliberation and increased attention to the content of communicated information (Ziegler et al., 2002).
text.formatted: An unreliable source on the other hand, invites more cognitive deliberation and increased attention to the content of communicated information <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Ziegler et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: That is because information communicated by untrustworthy sources is more likely to be viewed as potentially untrue, and therefore reasoners are situationally motivated to remain epistemically vigilant so as not to accept erroneous claims.
Political trust, when conceptualized as a source cue, should elicit a similar trustworthiness effect in argumentation from authority.
The proposed theoretical mechanism follows from previous studies.
That is, higher levels of political trust should reduce the perceived need to scrutinize whether reliance on cited political authorities is warranted.
Empirically, this should manifest as weak soundness discrimination.
As political trust increases, we therefore expect that people will evaluate sound arguments and fallacies in increasingly similar terms.
H2a: As political trust increases, individuals are less likely to distinguish sound arguments from fallacies.
Because we presume that politically trusting individuals will be less motivated to scrutinize the arguments, we also expect that they will be more susceptible to fallacies from authority.
H2b: As political trust increases, individuals are more likely to endorse fallacies from political authority.
So far, we have discussed our expectations for the overall effect of political trust on argument evaluation.
To understand the specific conditions that determine when and for whom this effect takes place, we turn to persuasion literature.
Studies on persuasive communication have been dominated by dual-process theories of cognition (Crano & Prislin, 2006; El Hedhli & Zourrig, 2023; Luttrell, 2018).
text.formatted: Studies on persuasive communication have been dominated by dual-process theories of cognition <ref type="bibr">(Crano & Prislin, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">El Hedhli & Zourrig, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Luttrell, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1984) is one such prominent example that falls under the dual-process umbrella.
text.formatted: The Elaboration Likelihood Model <ref type="bibr">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1984</ref>) is one such prominent example that falls under the dual-process umbrella.

text.text: The ELM identifies two distinct routes to persuasion with distinct cognitive implications.
The central route represents persuasion under high elaboration conditions -that is, when reasoners exert greater cognitive effort to process persuasive messages (Kitchen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The central route represents persuasion under high elaboration conditions -that is, when reasoners exert greater cognitive effort to process persuasive messages <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kitchen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, the peripheral route describes how persuasion occurs when elaboration is low.
These two routes do not represent a binary system of argument processing but rather idealized extremes across one elaboration continuum (O'Keefe, 2013).
text.formatted: These two routes do not represent a binary system of argument processing but rather idealized extremes across one elaboration continuum <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(O'Keefe, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The likelihood that one route is activated over the other varies as a function of processing motivation and cognitive ability (Petty & Wegener, 1999).
text.formatted: The likelihood that one route is activated over the other varies as a function of processing motivation and cognitive ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Petty & Wegener, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: When a reasoner is properly motivated and able to systematically analyze an argument, they are more likely to engage in elaboration and therefore more likely to process messages via the central route.
Previous studies have identified several factors that influence motivation and capacity including Need for Cognition, mood, affective response and distraction (Kitchen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Previous studies have identified several factors that influence motivation and capacity including Need for Cognition, mood, affective response and distraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kitchen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Among the most widely studied motivational influences in the ELM is the degree to which one feels personally involved with the topic that is discussed.

For example, elaboration likelihood is higher if the topic that is discussed is of high personal relevance to the reasoners, and if they as individuals have a higher propensity to engage in deep and intensive reasoning.
By contrast, if the topic leaves them disinterested and they are not particularly keen to think, then elaboration likelihood is low and by extension, the peripheral route is activated.

Because the two ELM routes imply entirely different degrees of argument scrutiny, they also imply that different argument features become more or less effective depending on the specific elaboration conditions.
Central-route persuasion involves extensive issue-relevant thinking and, as such, is highly sensitive to argument content and argument quality (Petty & Cacioppo, 1979).
text.formatted: Central-route persuasion involves extensive issue-relevant thinking and, as such, is highly sensitive to argument content and argument quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The ELM predicts that the more cognitively engaged an individual is, the more likely they are to be persuaded by strong arguments compared to weak ones.

Several studies offer empirical support for this prediction, suggesting that argument quality is a key determinant of persuasive outcomes achieved via the central route and that its persuasive value diminishes when the audience moves towards the peripheral end of the elaboration continuum (Andrews & Shimp, 1990; Breves et al., 2024; Carpenter, 2015; Cyr et al., 2018; Susmann et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Several studies offer empirical support for this prediction, suggesting that argument quality is a key determinant of persuasive outcomes achieved via the central route and that its persuasive value diminishes when the audience moves towards the peripheral end of the elaboration continuum <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andrews & Shimp, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Breves et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Carpenter, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cyr et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Susmann et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, peripheral-route persuasion relies on simple decision procedures that require little information processing (O'Keefe, 2013).
These procedures focus less on the communicated content within an argument and more on extrinsic argument features.
Source-related considerations are widely recognized as peripheral cues in ELM literature (Kitchen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Source-related considerations are widely recognized as peripheral cues in ELM literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kitchen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: As such, perceived source trustworthiness becomes more consequential for persuasion under low elaboration conditions.
However, the influence of source cues is not strictly constrained to the peripheral route.
ELM literature posits that one variable may serve multiple roles in persuasion depending on the amount of elaboration (Briñol & Petty, 2009; Petty & Briñol, 2014).
text.formatted: ELM literature posits that one variable may serve multiple roles in persuasion depending on the amount of elaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Briñol & Petty, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Petty & Briñol, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Under high elaboration conditions, source variables can themselves function as relevant arguments.
That is, reasoners take into account their impressions of argument sources as reasons for favouring or disfavouring a standpoint (Briñol & Petty, 2009).
text.formatted: That is, reasoners take into account their impressions of argument sources as reasons for favouring or disfavouring a standpoint <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Briñol & Petty, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: When an individual uses a source as an argument, they are inclined to carefully examine how the characteristics of this source relate to the advocated position and whether they sufficiently support the claim.

Although the ELM proposes different mechanisms through which source cues influence persuasion based on elaboration, both the aforementioned mechanisms lead to the same directional prediction in the context of the present study.
Previously, we hypothesized that political trust will predict the acceptability of authority arguments (H1) and patterns of soundness discrimination (H2).
Here, we propose that these effects will be stronger under low levels of political interest.
Drawing on the ELM, we treat political interest, i.e. the extent to which individuals are interested in politics, as a theoretically relevant variable to processing motivation.
We therefore expect that the influence of political trust on argument acceptability and soundness discrimination should depend on political interest.

Firstly, because the peripheral influence of trust decreases under high elaboration, politically interested individuals should rely less on their perceptions of the cited political authority and more on argument content.

Secondly, because trust serves as an argument under high elaboration, politically interested individuals should be more attuned to the relevance of source attributes for the acceptability of the claim.

Both of these mechanisms produce the same prediction: when they evaluate arguments from political authority, those with a strong interest in politics are less likely to be influenced by political trust and more likely distinguish between sound authority arguments and fallacies.
Accordingly, we formulate our third hypothesis:
H3: The positive association between political trust and evaluations of fallacious authority arguments will weaken as political interest increases.
In conceptualizing political trust as a source cue, we presume that it elicits similar epistemic effects to those associated with source trustworthiness in communication and persuasion research.
However, it is important to note that political trust differs from general source trustworthiness in one important aspect.

Source trustworthiness typically concerns the trust allocated to the specific source of a message, whereas political trust (in the way that it is typically measured) reflects an aggregated assessment across several political authorities.
Individuals with high levels of overall political trust can nevertheless regard a particular political institution as untrustworthy.

When that institution is invoked within an argument from authority, a high level of political trust may not predict either acceptance of the argument or the degree of scrutiny applied to its evaluation.
To account for this possibility, we need to distinguish between political trust as a generalized attitude and political trust as a distinct evaluative judgment for distinct political authorities.
To that effect, we draw on Easton's (1965; 1975) seminal work on the different types of political support.
text.formatted: To that effect, we draw on <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Easton's (1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">1975)</ref> seminal work on the different types of political support.

text.text: Easton distinguishes between diffuse and specific support, with the former reflecting a generalized attitude toward the political system as a whole and the latter describing trust as an object-specific attitude directed at particular institutions based on their individual performance.
Diffuse trust treats political systems as monolithic structures, wherein the trustworthiness of one type of authority can be inferred from the trustworthiness of another (Proszowska et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Diffuse trust treats political systems as monolithic structures, wherein the trustworthiness of one type of authority can be inferred from the trustworthiness of another <ref type="bibr">(Proszowska et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Specific trust, on the other hand, allows for the differentiation of political authorities as it is distinctly calibrated to the perceived trustworthiness of each particular entity (ibid.). Wu and Wilkes (2018) draw on Easton's diffuse-specific distinction to identify three types of political trusters: critical trusters, compliants, and cynics.
text.formatted: Specific trust, on the other hand, allows for the differentiation of political authorities as it is distinctly calibrated to the perceived trustworthiness of each particular entity (ibid.). <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Wu and Wilkes (2018)</ref> draw on Easton's diffuse-specific distinction to identify three types of political trusters: critical trusters, compliants, and cynics.

text.text: These profiles capture not only how much people trust political authorities, but also how they trust.
Compliants and cynics represent two opposing forms of diffuse political trust that differ primarily in their evaluative direction.
Both groups apply broadly consistent evaluations across political authorities; for compliants these evaluations are positive, whereas for cynics these evaluations are negative.
Critical trusters, by contrast, display specific trust.
Rather than generalizing their perceptions across institutions or leaders, they assess each political authority independently.
As a result, their trust in one authority does not automatically shape the perceived trustworthiness of others.
Our earlier predictions are rooted in the premise that political trust reflects a broader disposition toward political authorities.
While this assumption is informed by previous studies (Friesen et al., 2018; Hadarics, 2025), Easton's distinction proposes a more nuanced approach.
text.formatted: While this assumption is informed by previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Friesen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hadarics, 2025</ref>), Easton's distinction proposes a more nuanced approach.

text.text: Specifically, that this premise holds when trust is diffuse but not when trust is specific.
We therefore proceed to formulate an additional exploratory hypothesis: that trust differentiation reflects the extent to which one endorses a political entity by virtue of its authority status.

While H1 and H2 reflect our expectations for the overall effect of political trust on argument evaluation, we also hypothesize that this effect is moderated by trust differentiation as an empirical indicator consistent with specific-trust profiles.
We expect that as differentiation increases the effects predicted in H1 and H2 will be weaker whereas when differentiation is low these effects are stronger.
The effect of political trust on soundness discrimination will be stronger when trust differentiation is low rather than high.
To test our predictions regarding the influence of political trust on the persuasiveness of authority arguments, we conducted a pre-registered survey experiment.
Participants were asked to evaluate a series of political arguments which appealed to various authoritative sources in politics as a means to support the advanced standpoints.
Argument soundness was experimentally manipulated in accordance with the normative framework of pragma-dialectics.
We collected measures of political trust to test whether individual differences predicted argument acceptability (H1) and sensitivity to argument quality (H2).
We additionally measured political interest (H3) and trust differentiation (H4) as moderators of the trust effect.

A national Swedish sample of 1,010 adults (473 female, 535 male, 2 other; age range: 18-84 years, mean age = 55 years) was recruited through a third-party organization (Novus Research, a Swedish probability-based survey panel).

text.text: Probability-based sampling was employed to enhance representativeness (see: Supplementary Materials for detailed demographic information).
Our set of materials consisted of 12 arguments from authority, constructed by the authors for the purposes of this study.

To account for inter-item variation, the set included two versions of every original item (n = 6) with each version corresponding to one of two experimental conditions (sound vs. fallacious arguments).
Participants were presented with only one version of each argument.
The allocation of items to conditions was randomized on a per-participant basis and the overall set of the 6 selected arguments was equally distributed across the two soundness conditions.
The argumentative content was held constant in every item pair, meaning that the sound and fallacious iteration of an argument had the same premise and the same conclusion (see Table 1).
text.formatted: The argumentative content was held constant in every item pair, meaning that the sound and fallacious iteration of an argument had the same premise and the same conclusion (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Items within a pair differed in terms of the referenced authority, which determined whether the argument was normatively classified as sound or fallacious.
Specifically, we manipulated argument soundness by introducing either a match or a mismatch between the authority's domain and the domain of the topic under discussion.
All sound stimuli referenced political sources that possessed relevant epistemic authority to the issue at hand.
By contrast, all fallacious stimuli included inappropriate appeals to authority, either in the 'abuse of authority' variant or in the populist variant.

All appeals to authority across the two conditions included sources that could reasonably be regarded as authoritative in politics.
This design follows directly from our research aims.
We did not wish to contrast the persuasiveness of arguments appealing to authorities and arguments appealing to non-authorities.
Rather, our focus lies on whether participants infer epistemic authority from deontic sources, even when the source's authority is not relevant to the topic at hand.
To that end, authoritative standing was preserved in the sources of fallacious arguments and domain relevance was used as the benchmark for argument soundness.
In terms of content, the arguments were constructed to minimize the influence of prior policy attitudes and baseline disagreement with the conclusions.

The six selected argument topics (renewable energy, gender equality, education, healthcare, public infrastructure, and cybersecurity) were adapted from issues identified as important to the Swedish population in Novus Research's 2023 survey (Novus, 2024).

text.text: More importantly, both versions of each argument were grounded in policy positions expected to receive relatively broad public support (ibid.).

As such, differences in argument evaluation were less likely to reflect disagreement with the policy position itself and more likely to reflect participants' responses to the experimental manipulation.
The structure of the stimuli was heavily standardized.
Every argument contained one conclusion (the advocated claim) and one premise (the reasoning for accepting the claim) in a standard premise-therefore-conclusion order.

The types of statements used to construct premises and conclusions were similarly standardized, on the basis of a widely used typology in debate theory (Freeley & Steinberg, 2008; Inch & Warnick, 1989) which distinguishes between statements of fact (F), statements of value (V) and statements of policy (P).

text.text: Of these three types, F and P statements are of relevance to our stimuli.
F statements contain factual observations, i.e. they state what is.
P statements contain proposed actions, i.e. they state what should be done.
All items included in our stimulus set contained an F statement as a premise (X said Y) and a P statement as a conclusion (therefore Y should be implemented).

Despite linguistically grounding the materials to preserve naturalistic argumentative conditions, the use of the FP statement type configuration allowed us to uphold a high degree of standardization across items.
Argument evaluation was measured on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (not convincing at all) to 7 (extremely convincing).
We measured political trust using a 5-items scale adapted from the European Social Survey (2018; 2020) and the Eurobarometer (2023).

Participants were asked to indicate their trust to several political institutions (the Police, Courts of Justice, the Media, the Government, Political Parties) on an 11-point scale, with responses ranging from "do not trust at all" (0) to "completely trust" (10).
We calculated the mean score across all items as an index of overall political trust.
The five-item scale showed good internal consistency in our sample (Cronbach's α = .76, 95% CI [.74, .78]).
Trust differentiation was subsequently operationalized as the standard deviation of each participant's trust ratings across the five institutions.

Higher values indicate greater variability in trust across institutional targets, reflecting a tendency to discriminate between political authorities rather than applying uniform evaluations across them.
Lower values indicate more uniform trust ratings, consistent with a diffuse orientation toward political authority.
This approach treats within-person variability in trust ratings as a continuous index of evaluative discrimination Political interest Political interest was measured with a single self-report item.
Responses were registered on a 4-point scale ranging from 1 ("not at all interested") to 4 ("extremely interested"; Prior, 2010; Stromback et al., 2013).

text.text: Given that outcomes of political communication are often subject to ideological differences, we measured participants' political ideology for inclusion as a control variable in our analyses.
We asked participants to self-place along two 11-point scales (ranging from "left" to "right" and "progressive" to "conservative") to indicate their political ideology (Jost et al., 2009).
text.formatted: We asked participants to self-place along two 11-point scales (ranging from "left" to "right" and "progressive" to "conservative") to indicate their political ideology <ref type="bibr">(Jost et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Following our pre-registration, we used the mean across the two items as a composite score for political ideology (ρ = .69).
Demographic variables were collected, including gender (coded as1 = male,2 = female,3 = other), age, and educational background.
Education was assessed using detailed items asking about participants' current study level or highest completed education, with responses ranging from primary through tertiary education.
These were recoded into three more balanced ISCED categories: primary/lower secondary education, upper secondary education and higher education.
Data collection was conducted by Novus Research in February 2026, using a Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (CAWI) procedure.
All subjects gave informed consent prior to participation.
Prior to the task, we administered a set of instructions aiming to guide evaluation towards argument soundness and away from agreement-based considerations.
Participants were told that in each argument, the speaker expressed an opinion and cited other people's claims as reasons for holding this opinion.
They were then instructed to assign ratings focusing on whether the reason provided a convincing justification for the opinion.
We explicitly instructed participants to disregard their personal views on the topics discussed.
Following participation, participants were debriefed on the design and aims of the research.
The design, hypotheses and planned analyses were preregistered on OSF Hypotheses 1-3 were formally preregistered, while Hypothesis 4 is considered exploratory.

text.text: As a general trend, sound arguments were evaluated more favorably than fallacious arguments, although the effect did not reach conventional levels of statistical significance (b = 0.43, SE = 0.24, 95% CI[-0.03, 0.9], p = .10).
Crucially, there was no evidence that political trust moderated the effect of argument soundness, indicated by a nonsignificant interaction term (b = -0.01, SE = 0.02, 95% CI[-0.06, 0.03], p = .49).
Both the relative magnitude of these effects and their statistical significance was robust to the inclusion of sociodemographic and ideological covariates in the controlled model.
Because the sound and fallacious arguments constituted matched pairs across six argumentative topics, we inspected stimulus heterogeneity with topic as the grouping variable.

We used the emmeans (Lenth, 2025) package in RStudio to examine topic-specific contrasts and found that, across all item pairs, sound arguments were evaluated more favorably than fallacies, although the magnitude of this effect varied across topics (see: Supplementary Materials).

text.text: Given the observed heterogeneity in the soundness effect across stimulus pairs, we estimated an additional linear mixed-effects model for the trust x soundness interaction, with a random soundness slope per topic.
This specification was not included in our pre-registration and is reported as a robustness check accounting for stimulus-level heterogeneity.
In this model, sound arguments were evaluated significantly more favorably than fallacious arguments (b = 0.43, SE = 0.11, 95% CI[0.19, 0.67], p = .013).

Importantly, the political trust x soundness interaction remained non-significant (b = -0.015, SE = 0.021, 95% CI[-0.06, 0.03], p = .49), including after adjustment for age, gender, education, and political ideology.
Overall, political trust predicted more favorable evaluations of authority-based arguments but did not predict lower sensitivity to argument soundness as expected.

To test whether the relationship between political trust and argument evaluation varied as a function of political interest and argument soundness, we estimated a linear mixed-effects model including argument evaluation as an outcome variable predicted by political trust, political interest, argument soundness and their interactions, with random intercepts for participants and items.
Analyses were conducted in RStudio using the lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) and emmeans (Lenth, 2025) packages.

text.text: The focal three-way interaction was statistically significant (b = -0.057, SE = 0.025, 95% CI[-0.11, -0.01], p = .022).

The interaction remained virtually unchanged after adjustment for age, political ideology, gender, and education and under the alternative topic-based randomeffects specification (see: Supplementary Materials).

As preregistered, we probed this interaction by estimating the effect of political trust on discrimination between sound and fallacious arguments at low (-1 SD) and high (+1 SD) levels of political interest.
At low political interest, political trust was not significantly associated with soundness discrimination (Δb = 0.027, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [-0.029, 0.083], p = .344).

However, at high political interest greater political trust was associated with weaker discrimination between sound and fallacious arguments (Δb = -0.060, SE = 0.028, 95% CI [-0.116, -0.005], p = .034).

Moreover, the difference between these effects was statistically significant (Δb = -0.087, SE = 0.038, 95% CI [-0.162, -0.013], p = .022) suggesting that political trust differentially predicts soundness discrimination depending on political interest.
At higher political interest evaluative accuracy decreases as trust increases whereas this association does not emerge at low political interest.
Further probing indicated that this interaction was driven by fallacious arguments.

Political trust was more strongly associated with favorable evaluations of fallacious arguments at high (b= 0.184) than at low (b= 0.069) levels of political interest, a difference that was statistically significant (Δb = 0.115, SE = 0.040, 95% CI [0.036, 0.194], p = 0.004).
Conversely, its association with evaluations of sound arguments did not significantly differ between highand low-interest participants (Δb = 0.027, SE = 0.040, 95% CI [-0.052, 0.106], p = 0.498).

Thus, although political interest moderated the relationship between political trust and sensitivity to argument soundness, the pattern was opposite to the hypothesized direction: political trust was more strongly associated with favorable evaluations of fallacious arguments among participants with higher, rather than lower, political interest.

To examine whether trust differentiation moderated the trust effect on argument soundness, we estimated a mixed-effects linear regression model with random intercepts for participants and items predicting argument evaluation from political trust, argument soundness, trust differentiation, and their interaction.

Consistent with our exploratory fourth hypothesis, the trust x soundness interaction was qualified by a significant three-way interaction with trust differentiation (b = 0.07, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.12], p = 0.02).

This effect remained significant in the controlled model and the alternative random slope models, indicating that the interaction was robust to demographic and ideological adjustments as well as stimulus heterogeneity.
To interpret this interaction, we estimated conditional slopes of political trust for sound and fallacious arguments at low (-1 SD) and high (+1 SD) levels of trust differentiation using emtrends.
The association between political trust and soundness discrimination differed significantly between low and high differentiation (Δb = 0.11, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.018, 0.198], p = 0.02).

At low differentiation, the political-trust slope was slightly weaker for sound arguments (b = 0.115) than for fallacies (b = 0.156), although this difference was not statistically significant (Δb = -0.041, p = 0.155).

At high differentiation, the political-trust slope was stronger for sound arguments (b = 0.14) than for fallacies (b = 0.08), with the difference approaching conventional statistical significance (Δb = 0.067, p = 0.060).
Figure 3 illustrates this pattern.
As trust differentiation increased, the association between political trust and discrimination between sound and fallacious arguments became more positive.
Throughout this study, we conceptualized political trust as a source cue in political argumentation from authority.
Consistent with this premise, political trust emerged as a reliable predictor of argument acceptability across all tested models.
What our data did not support, however, is the hypothesis that trust as a source cue determines patterns of soundness discrimination.
While participants who overall trusted institutions more also tended to be more receptive to political arguments from authority, they were no less able to distinguish sound arguments from fallacies.
We thus find no evidence that political trust compromises evaluative accuracy in authority argumentation.
This does not, however, imply a total absence of trustrelated complications.
One rather surprising finding was the moderating role of political interest.

Even though the effect of political trust on soundness discrimination varied across different levels of interest, the direction of this effect was opposite to what we had anticipated in our third hypothesis.
Our prediction, informed by the ELM, was that greater interest in the topic of argumentation should predict more soundness-driven evaluations.
On the contrary, we found that high-trust participants who also reported a strong interest in politics exhibited weaker soundness discrimination and greater endorsement of fallacies.
In other words, evaluation became less normatively accurate and more subject to the influence of trust as political interest increased.

Interpreted against our earlier findings, it seems that political trust has a general persuasive function in political communication and that this persuasive function can interfere with soundness-based evaluation specifically under high levels of political interest.

Driven by the discrepancy between our original hypothesis and our findings, we begin to speculate on the direction of the moderation by revisiting the theoretical implications of political interest as a proxy for processing motivation.
According to the ELM, argument quality becomes more consequential as individuals move toward the central end of the elaboration continuum.
This is a key theoretical premise in traditional dual-process accounts, where accuracy-driven processing is associated with increased cognitive reflection.
This premise has received substantial empirical support, and the pattern was found to replicate within political communicative settings as well (Aspernäs et al., 2023; Pennycook & Rand, 2019).

text.text: Interpreting new information in attitudinally consistent ways requires deep, effortful processing.
As such, and contrary to traditional dual-process approaches, high elaboration conditions could in fact facilitate biased conclusions (Seremeta et al., 2023).

text.text: This approach may be a possible explanation for the weaker soundness discrimination we observed among highly interested participants.
Nonetheless, such an explanation implies that a simple source-cue account on political trust does not sufficiently explain the full pattern.
Instead, our findings on the moderation of political interest appear more consistent with trust as a motivational influence.
Read this way, our results do not contradict ELM theory.
In line with the ELM's multiple roles postulate, source cues can serve several different functions depending on the amount of elaboration (Briñol & Petty, 2009; Petty & Briñol, 2014).

text.text: We have already mentioned that source factors function as a peripheral cue when elaboration is low but can serve as arguments when elaboration is high.

The model also holds that under high elaboration source cues can additionally "motivate or enable people to either support or derogate the content of the information provided" (Briñol & Petty, 2009, p. 59).

text.text: Put simply, source cues may bias the direction of argument evaluation when processing occurs via the central route.
This is an equivalent mechanism to the one discussed earlier, where cognitive reflection was shown to encourage biased thinking rather than correct it (Kahan, 2013).

text.text: Hence, a motivational explanation for the role of political interest in our study is supported by empirical research on motivated cognition as well as by ELM theory.
More importantly, ELM's multiple-roles postulate allows us to move beyond a narrow conceptualization of political trust as either a source cue or a motivational influence.
Such a unidimensional interpretation cannot sufficiently explain the pattern of findings observed in our study.
The analyses for H1 and H2 are consistent with a source-cue account, in that political trust predicted argument acceptability even though did not predict indiscriminate acceptance.
The unexpected moderation observed for H3, however, raises the possibility that the role of political trust changes under conditions of strong political interest.
Taken together, these findings suggest that political trust could play multiple roles in political argumentation from authority.
While it may generally operate as a favorable source-related influence, it can also become implicated in directional processing under particular conditions.
Our exploratory analysis of trust differentiation provides a further, though tentative, indication that the relationship between political trust and soundness discrimination is conditional.

At low levels of trust dispersion, political trust was negatively associated with evaluative accuracy whereas the same association did not emerge when individuals differentiated their trust judgments more strongly across institutions.

One possible interpretation for this finding is that dispersion patterns reflect the distinction between political trust as a generalized attitude and political trust as an institution-specific judgment.

From this perspective, the effect of trust as a generalized attitude is more consistent with a motivational influence account, whereas institution-specific trust appears to align more with a simple sourcerelated influence.
Here, it is important to note that our dispersion analysis can only capture metric differences rather than evaluative processes.
For example, a participant with a low differentiation score may nevertheless have produced institution-specific judgments.

While in our study, differentiation measures do not account for the cognitive mechanisms involved in political trust calibration, they may point to an additional boundary condition for the motivational role of trust in political communication.
The current research offers a nuanced understanding of political trust as a communicative cue, with implications for critical citizenship.
We find that trusting citizens are inclined to engage with political institutions in good faith, without blindly accepting the claims and decisions made by these institutions.
However, we also identify certain conditions where political trust positively predicts the acceptance of authority arguments even when they contain pragmatic irregularities.
We therefore conclude this paper without assigning specific democratic correlates to political trust.
Rather, we propose that its democratic implications may depend on when and how confidence in political institutions enters citizens' evaluations of political claims.

Understanding these conditions is essential for a broader account of political trust that recognizes both its role in sustaining cooperation with political institutions and the continued importance of critical scrutiny toward political authority.
This study offers a novel understanding of political trust as a cue in political communication, however, certain limitations should be acknowledged.

Prior attitudes may therefore constitute an important boundary condition for evaluative accuracy, particularly given our proposed motivational interpretation of the conditional effects of political trust.

The present design allows us to estimate the relationship between political trust and argument evaluation across a range of political topics, but it cannot determine whether this relationship varies as a function of agreement with the argument's conclusion.

Future research should thus measure or experimentally vary prior policy attitudes to examine whether political trust differentially shapes the evaluation of attitude-congruent and attitude-incongruent arguments from authority.
Second, our hypothesis on the moderating role of political interest was informed by ELM literature.
Political interest in this context constitutes a theoretically relevant variable to processing motivation.
However, our measures do not directly account for cognitive elaboration and processing effort.

While our interpretation of the findings remains theoretically grounded, it cannot definitively establish the underlying cognitive mechanism.Further research is needed to demonstrate that the conditional pattern observed here reflects changes in elaboration likelihood.
Lastly, the institutional context of the study should be considered when assessing the generalizability of our findings.

Although the probability-based Swedish sample strengthens population-level inference within this context, the meaning and consequences of political trust are embedded in broader political and institutional environments.
Future studies should therefore examine whether the relationships observed here generalize across political systems characterized by different levels and configurations of institutional trust.
